cues.text: In this town,
every kid got a monster egg on their tenth birthday.
You see, nobody knew where the eggs came from.
Every spring, they just appeared in the old stone nest at the edge of town,
one for every child,
and the weird part was that nobody had ever seen who left them there.
Our whole town ran on monsters.
Dragons lit the ovens at the bakery,
a phoenix carried the mail,
and big stone golems carried sleepy kids to school.
Every monster wore its rank on a wooden sign,
and the higher the rank, the more the town loved you.
My best friend hatched a dragon.
Rank one million.
My sister hatched a phoenix.
Rank ten thousand.
It was actually a pretty good place to grow up,
but there was one problem I could not stop thinking about.
My egg was broken.
It was grey and cold, with a big crack down the middle.
When I showed the adults,
they told me a cracked egg was a dead egg.
They said I should throw it in the old well, like all the others.
But that only made me hold it tighter.
Sometimes, late at night, I would hear a soft tapping from inside the shell.
Tap. Tap. Tap.
But every time I lit a torch to look,
it stopped before I could see what was making it.
One day, I asked the oldest woman in town if a cracked egg had ever hatched.
She stared at my egg for a long time before whispering,
"I forgot the reason. I only remember the rule. Never keep one."
Then she walked away.
That night, I couldn't sleep.
Why would a whole town be afraid of one broken egg,
unless something was still alive inside it?
So, I decided to hatch it myself.
First, I tried keeping it warm.
I wrapped it in blankets
and sat on it like a chicken for three whole days.
Nothing hatched, and the only thing that cracked was my back.
The whole town laughed at me,
but I was not done.
If blankets wouldn't work, I needed something hotter.
So every day, I hid the egg in my backpack
and sat as close to my best friend's dragon as I could.
After weeks of waiting, the dragon finally sneezed.
The fire hit my egg,
and the egg drank it. Every last spark.
Then the crack started to glow.
But there was a catch. One sneeze was not enough.
My egg needed more fire than every dragon in town could make,
and there was only one place with that much fire:
the lava lake outside the wall,
where no kid had ever been allowed to go.
So I filled my backpack: bread, water, a rope, and a torch.
And one more thing: my blanket,
in case the thing inside was cold when it came out.
My best friend caught me at the gate and begged me to stay.
"What if something bad comes out?" he asked.
"Then at least it won't hatch alone," I said.
The next morning, I climbed over the wall
and walked to the edge of the lava.
The heat was so strong, the soles of my shoes began to smoke.
I turned around for one last look at home.
Dragons were lighting the ovens,
golems were carrying kids to school,
and somewhere, my sister's phoenix was delivering the mail.
Not one of them knew what I was holding.
I hugged my egg, took a deep breath,
and let it go.
For a second, I was sure I had destroyed it.
The egg sank without a sound.
Then the whole lake went dark,
as if something had swallowed all the fire.
The ground began to shake,
the shell split open,
and out crawled the smallest monster I had ever seen.
A worm. Rank one.
I carried it home in my blanket, and the whole town laughed,
until the worm made one tiny sound.
Every dragon stopped.
Every phoenix landed.
And one by one, every monster in town turned to the wall,
and bowed.
Then the sky went dark,
and something bigger than our whole town landed on the wall.
And that was when I finally understood the rule.
The eggs in the stone nest were never gifts.
Our golems had been stealing them.
A cracked egg is not broken.
It is a baby, calling for its mother.
And mine had just called her home.
Subscribe before she finds me.
